metadata.title: Subacute encephalomyelitis presenting as stiff-person syndrome: clinical, polygraphic, and pathologic correlations.
metadata.abstract: A 60-year-old woman presented with stiff-person syndrome (SPS). Treatment with diazepam controlled her painful spasms initially. Two and one-half years after the onset of SPS, new spells of paroxysmal leg jerking and apnea developed. A spell was recorded with simultaneous video and polygraphic techniques that revealed simultaneous firing of motor unit potentials in several muscles (paraspinal, internal hamstring, and abdominal muscles). Apnea was associated with arterial oxygen desaturation. An increase in the dose of diazepam decreased the number and severity of these episodes. Seventeen months later, the patient began to taper the diazepam dose. Shortly thereafter, she had a cardiorespiratory arrest and subsequently died. Autopsy showed small chronic inflammatory foci in the pancreas (some associated with islets) and findings of diffuse encephalomyelitis characterized by perivascular cuffing in the spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala and a dense mononuclear infiltrate in the anterior horns of the lumbar and cervical cord, with relative preservation of axons and myelin. Cell typing showed this infiltrate was polyclonal and reactive. There have been rare cases of SPS associated with encephalomyelitis reported previously. Although the prolonged course in our patient suggested that SPS may have preceded encephalomyelitis, the more likely explanation is that the patient had an unusually long course of encephalomyelitis alone.

Syndrome: Clinical, Polygraphic, and

Summary: A 60-year-old woman presented with stiff- 
person syndrome (SPS). Treatment with diazepam con- 
trolled her painful spasms initially. Two and one-half 
years after the onset of SPS, new spells of paroxysmal leg 
jerking and apnea developed. A spell was recorded with 
simultaneous video and polygraphic techniques that re- 
vealed simultaneous firing of motor unit potentials in sev- 
eral muscles (paraspinal, internal hamstring, and abdom- 
inal muscles). Apnea was associated with arterial oxygen 
desaturation. An increase in the dose of diazepam de- 
creased the number and severity of these episodes. Sev- 
enteen months later, the patient began to taper the diaz- 
epam dose, Shortly thereafter, she had a cardiorespirato- 
ry arrest and subsequently died. Autopsy showed small 
chronic inflammatory foci in the pancreas (some associ- 
ated with islets) and findings of diffuse encephalomyelitis 
characterized by perivascular cuffing in the spinal cord, 
brainstem, thalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala and a 
dense mononuclear infiltrate in the anterior horns of the 
lumbar and cervical cord, with relative preservation of 
axons and myelin. Cell typing showed this infiltrate was 
polyclonal and reactive. There have been rare cases of 
SPS associated with encephalomyelitis reported previ- 
ously. Although the prolonged course in our patient sug- 
gested that SPS may have preceded encephalomyelitis, 
the more likely explanation is that the patient had an un- 
usually long course of encephalomyelitis alone. Key

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) was first described 
by Moersch and Woltman (1) in 1956 as a syndrome 
of “progressive, fluctuating muscular rigidity and 
spasms.” Howard (2) in 1963 reported the use of 
diazepam in the successful treatment of the syn-

drome. Subsequently, baclofen (3,4), sodium val- 
proate (S), and cortisol replacement in a corticotro- 
pin-deficient patient (6) also have been shown to be 
useful treatments. More recently, evidence has 
been presented that an autoimmune mechanism 
may underlie some (7,s) but not all (9) cases of SPS. 
Plasmapheresis has resulted in remission in one pa- 
tient (10). 
There have been two reports of myoclonus oc- 
curring in patients with SPS (1 1,12), giving rise to 
the term “jerking stiff-man syndrome. ” Sudden 
death has been reported in patients with SPS. The 
mechanism has not been explained (13,14), al- 
though autonomic instability has been suspected 
(15). The relationship between SPS and encephalo- 
myelitis has not been resolved (1s-18); this is partly 
because of the rarity of these conditions. 
We describe a patient who presented with SPS,

albeit with some atypical features, who developed 
unusual spells of paroxysmal leg jerking and apnea. 
A typical spell was documented on video with si- 
multaneous polygraphic recording of electroen- 
cephalographic, surface electromyographic, and re- 
spiratory functions. Encephalomyelitis was con- 
firmed at autopsy. By placing this well documented 
case in the public domain, we hope to facilitate the 
recognition of this condition and its correct diagno- 
sis. 
CASE REPORT 
A 60-year-old woman began having severe bilat- 
eral paroxysmal foot pain with associated “curling 
up” of her toes and feet (the right foot was affected 
more than the left); these symptoms slowly became 
worse. Painful spasms then involved the buttocks, 
thighs, and calves and sometimes caused her to 
walk stiff-legged. These spasms affected her bal- 
ance and resulted in several falls. The spasms typ- 
ically were aggravated by apprehension and embar- 
rassment or by the attention of other people. The 
severity of spasms tended to lessen when she was 
relaxed around her family. Occasionally, spasms 
awakened her at night. The spasms became more 
frequent and intense over time. Magnetic resonance 
imaging of the entire spine showed no abnormali- 
ties. 
One year after symptom onset, she was hospital- 
ized because of attacks of extensor rigidity of her 
lower extremities. Between attacks, the neurologic 
examination revealed normal strength in all extrem- 
ities and normal sensation. The muscle stretch re- 
flexes were increased at the knees but were de- 
pressed at both ankles, and the plantar responses 
were flexor. There were no abnormal findings in the 
upper extremities, and the cranial nerves were in- 
tact. coordination was normal in the upper extrem- 
ities but difficult to assess in the lower extremities 
because of extensor rigidity. While she was hospi- 
talized, severe extensor spasms of the lower ex- 
tremities, lasting hours at a time, were observed. 
Plain films of the spine showed straightening of the 
lumbar lordosis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was 
clear. Glucose concentration was 78 mg/dl and total 
protein 81 mg/dl. The concentration of total white 
cells was 2.6/~1 (polymorphs, 0.3/p.1; lymphocytes, 
2.01~1; monocytes, 0.3/pl) and of erythrocytes 
4,779/~1. The CSF index was 0.60 (normal 0-0.77). 
One oligoclonal band was present in the CSF, and 
one oligoclonal band was present in the serum. 
These findings were considered consistent with a 
traumatic lumbar puncture. The serum creatine ki- 
nase concentration was 102 U/L (normal 38-176 
U/L). Diazepam, up to 10 mg three times a day, 
relieved the spasms. Eighteen and 24 months after 
the onset of her symptoms, her L4 and L2 vertebrae 
collapsed. This was thought to be the result of lum- 
bar paraspinal muscle spasms on osteoporotic ver- 
tebrae. A diagnosis of SPS was made. 
At age 62 years, 2.5 years after the onset of SPS, 
she presented because of the onset of new spells of 
shaking during which she became short of breath 
and her toes became dusky blue. These spells usu- 
ally occurred while she was attempting to move and 
were precipitated by anxiety. She was treated by 
increasing the diazepam dosage to 30,35, and 40 mg 
three times a day, each time with initial control and 
subsequent breakthrough of the spells. Ten months 
after the onset of the shaking spells, the patient was 
hospitalized for further evaluation, initially in an 
intensive care unit. The CSF was clear. Glucose 
concentration was 74 mg/dl and total protein 40 mg/ 
dl. The concentration of total white cells was 1 .O/p.l 
(neutrophils, 7%; lymphocytes, 88%; monocytes, 
5%) and of erythrocytes 6/pL No blasts or malig- 
nant cells were seen. The CSF index was 0.48. The 
CSF IgG synthesis rate was 0.00 (normal 0-8 mg/24 
h). Four oligoclonal bands were present in both the 
CSF and the serum. Tests for antibodies for glu- 
tamic acid decarboxylase were not performed on 
either serum or CSF, and unfortunately samples 
were not saved. Two typical spells were precipi- 
tated by having her get out of bed and walk with 
support. The stimulus for the spell was allowing her 
to bear her own weight. She would stiffen, and her 
legs and spine would shake uncontrollably. After 
she was placed back in bed, the leg shaking contin- 
ued; she fanned herself with her hands, uttered 
words such as “fan me,” and was able to count 
while becoming progressively dusky blue in the 
face, fingers, and toes. Determination of blood 
gases on blood drawn from an indwelling arterial 
line during the course of these two spells showed 
that the patient had significantly desaturated arte- 
rial oxygen concentration (Table 1). Her baseline 
metabolic status on admission and at dismissal was 
alkalotic. 
A video recording of a third typical spell with 
simultaneous polygraph monitoring showed that it 
began with disrupted regular breathing and in- 
creased muscular activity in the internal hamstrings 
and abdominal muscles (Fig. 1A and B), findings 
corresponding to initial myoclonic activity in the

legs. Repetitive firing of muscles then increased in 
amplitude and frequency and spread to cervical 
paraspinal and all the scalp muscles. Only a few 
muscles were sampled for the polygraph recording. 
When the spell was fully developed, most muscles 
were involved (see video). In the early part of the 
spell, muscles fired synchronously at a rate of -2-3 
Hz. This rate then increased to 9 Hz, and breathing 
stopped (Fig. 1B and C). 
One hundred seconds into the spell, the patient 
was able to count from 1 to 10, despite the absence 
of spontaneous respiratory movements (Fig. 1D). 
Esophageal manometry showed that she accom- 
plished this by increasing her intrathoracic pres- 
sure, exhaling against a closed glottis, and then 
emitting the air to articulate the numbers-this was 
reminiscent of coughing, but without initial inhala- 
tion. 
Palpation of the patient’s abdomen 140 s into the 
spell resulted in some attenuation in the frequency 
of muscle firing at all spinal levels, with resumption 
of high-frequency firing after the abdomen was re- 
leased (Fig. 1E). The heart rate, which was 108 
beatshin when the spell began, was 84 beatshin at 
the time the stomach was palpated, despite the 
stress of the spell and profound oxygen desatura- 
tion. The spell terminated abruptly after 163 s, and 
respirations resumed at a rate of 38 breathshin 
(Fig. 1F). The electroencephalogram showed gen- 
eralized slowing of the background to 5-6 Hz, con- 
sistent with the patient’s hypoxemia at this stage, 
and was back to normal within 2 min. At the end of 
the spell, the patient was exhausted but responsive. 
She was dismissed and instructed to take 80 mg of 
diazepam four times a day, and, at this dose, was 
able to walk with minimal support without precipi- 
tating spells. However, she continued to have tonic 
spells, consisting of spasms of her axial and lower 
extremity muscles, occurring every 1-2 weeks. 
When evaluated 4 months later, she had her worst- 
ever leg-shaking apneic spell, the first since her dis- 
missal. It began as she walked into the physician’s 
office. At its worst, she was unresponsive, although 
her pulse was steady throughout. Diazepam was 
continued. However, because of the onset of mem- 
ory problems, the patient began tapering the diaze- 
pam on her own and decreased it gradually to 50- 
60-50-60 mg a day. Three and one-half months later, 
2 weeks following her most recent tonic spell, her 
husband found her unresponsive and slumped over 
the breakfast table without a pulse or respirations. 
She was resuscitated but never regained conscious- 
ness, and she was declared brain dead 8 days later. 
General Pathologic Findings 
Abnormalities were limited to the heart and the 
pancreas. There were cardiomegaly , probably sec- 
ondary to hypertension, and minimal atherosclero- 
sis. Pancreatic architecture was preserved overall. 
There were small foci of chronic inflammatory cells 
that included both lymphocytes and plasma cells. 
Some, but not all, of these chronic inflammatory 
foci appeared to be associated with islets. 
Neuropathologic Findings 
Routine and special histopathologic stains per- 
formed on spinal cord and brain tissue obtained at 
autopsy showed two major findings: The most strik- 
ing abnormality was a dense infiltrate in the anterior 
horn of the lumbar spinal cord. Larger motor neu- 
rons in the central portions of the anterior horns on 
both sides showed chromatolysis of swollen cyto- 
plasm, a mild to moderate degree of eosinophilia, 
and eccentric, often barely visible, nuclei (Fig. 2). 
Fairly good preservation of cell outlines of these 
motor neurons was shown with the Bielschowsky 
stain. There was a dense infiltrate consisting of 
small monocytic cells, microglial cells, and a few 
small rounded macrophages against a background 
of neuropil changes consisting mostly of myelin loss

with relative preservation of axons, although some 
of the latter showed diffuse enlargement. Small 
blood vessels with hypertrophied endothelial cells 
were prominent. A few blood vessels at the more 
peripheral portion of the anterior horns, in the pos- 
terior horns, and rarely elsewhere, including the 
subarachnoid space, exhibited mild to moderate 
perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. A much 
milder form of the anterior horn changes noted in 
the lumbar segments was seen at the cervical level. 
Glial fibrillary astrocytic protein immunohisto- 
chemical stain revealed diffuse astrocytosis of the 
gray matter surrounding areas of increased cellular- 
ity and neuronal degeneration. No distinct evidence 
of descending or ascending tract degeneration was 
observed. Immunoperoxidase methods (19) and 
DNA probes with hybridization techniques (20) 
showed the lymphocytic infiltrate to be a polyclonal 
T-cell and B-cell response without evidence of ma- 
lignancy. 
Also, mild to moderate perivascular lymphocytic 
infiltration was present in the amygdala, hippocam- 
pus, basal ganglia, thalamus and hypothalamus, 
midbrain, and pontine tegmentum. There were ill 
defined areas of a mild fibrillary astrocytosis in the 
hypothalamus and the tegmentum of midbrain, 
pons, and medulla. There was no neuronophagia, 
overt loss of neurons, or microglial nodule forma- 
tion. The only other abnormality was that of respi- 
rator brain, consistent with the terminal history of 
cardiac arrest and survival on a respirator for 8 
days. 
DISCUSSION 
We initially hypothesized that although SPS and 
encephalomyelitis usually occur independently of 
each other, occasionally encephalomyelitis may de- 
velop in a patient with SPS. SPS preceded the de- 
velopment of features of encephalomyelitis at least 
in one (15) of two previously reported patients 
(15,17) in whom the two conditions may have co- 
existed. An alternative hypothesis, more parsimo- 
nious, is that some patients with encephalomyelitis 
might have clinical features, at presentation, sug- 
gesting a diagnosis of SPS. 
According to the first hypothesis, if a patient has 
SPS alone, the course is usually indolent (1,21). En- 
cephalomyelitis alone has a rapidly progressive and 
fatal course, regardless of the presence or absence 
of rigidity or of underlying neoplasm (22-25). On 
the basis of this hypothesis, if encephalomyelitis 
develops in a patient with SPS, the course is ex- 
pected to be intermediate: It is relatively benign as 
long as features of SPS predominate (making SPS 
the patient’s diagnosis at the time) and becomes 
malignant when encephalomyelitis supervenes. 
The pathologic features of the two conditions, in 
isolation, are different. Five patients with SPS have 
been reported in whom the spinal cord was exam- 
ined at autopsy (15,2628). The spinal cord in four 
patients showed a slight pallor of the dorsal column, 
loss of Nissl substance in some anterior horn cells 
with shrinkage of the cytoplasm, increased numbers 
of glial nuclei (26), slightly decreased motor neu- 
rons in the lateral nuclei of the central horn at the

(15). The relationship between SPS and encephalo- 
myelitis has not been resolved (1s-18); this is partly 
because of the rarity of these conditions. 
We describe a patient who presented with SPS,

albeit with some atypical features, who developed 
unusual spells of paroxysmal leg jerking and apnea. 
A typical spell was documented on video with si- 
multaneous polygraphic recording of electroen- 
cephalographic, surface electromyographic, and re- 
spiratory functions. Encephalomyelitis was con- 
firmed at autopsy. By placing this well documented 
case in the public domain, we hope to facilitate the 
recognition of this condition and its correct diagno- 
sis. 
CASE REPORT 
A 60-year-old woman began having severe bilat- 
eral paroxysmal foot pain with associated “curling 
up” of her toes and feet (the right foot was affected 
more than the left); these symptoms slowly became 
worse. Painful spasms then involved the buttocks, 
thighs, and calves and sometimes caused her to 
walk stiff-legged. These spasms affected her bal- 
ance and resulted in several falls. The spasms typ- 
ically were aggravated by apprehension and embar- 
rassment or by the attention of other people. The 
severity of spasms tended to lessen when she was 
relaxed around her family. Occasionally, spasms 
awakened her at night. The spasms became more 
frequent and intense over time. Magnetic resonance 
imaging of the entire spine showed no abnormali- 
ties. 
One year after symptom onset, she was hospital- 
ized because of attacks of extensor rigidity of her 
lower extremities. Between attacks, the neurologic 
examination revealed normal strength in all extrem- 
ities and normal sensation. The muscle stretch re- 
flexes were increased at the knees but were de- 
pressed at both ankles, and the plantar responses 
were flexor. There were no abnormal findings in the 
upper extremities, and the cranial nerves were in- 
tact. coordination was normal in the upper extrem- 
ities but difficult to assess in the lower extremities 
because of extensor rigidity. While she was hospi- 
talized, severe extensor spasms of the lower ex- 
tremities, lasting hours at a time, were observed. 
Plain films of the spine showed straightening of the 
lumbar lordosis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was 
clear. Glucose concentration was 78 mg/dl and total 
protein 81 mg/dl. The concentration of total white 
cells was 2.6/~1 (polymorphs, 0.3/p.1; lymphocytes, 
2.01~1; monocytes, 0.3/pl) and of erythrocytes 
4,779/~1. The CSF index was 0.60 (normal 0-0.77). 
One oligoclonal band was present in the CSF, and 
one oligoclonal band was present in the serum. 
These findings were considered consistent with a 
traumatic lumbar puncture. The serum creatine ki- 
nase concentration was 102 U/L (normal 38-176 
U/L). Diazepam, up to 10 mg three times a day, 
relieved the spasms. Eighteen and 24 months after 
the onset of her symptoms, her L4 and L2 vertebrae 
collapsed. This was thought to be the result of lum- 
bar paraspinal muscle spasms on osteoporotic ver- 
tebrae. A diagnosis of SPS was made. 
At age 62 years, 2.5 years after the onset of SPS, 
she presented because of the onset of new spells of 
shaking during which she became short of breath 
and her toes became dusky blue. These spells usu- 
ally occurred while she was attempting to move and 
were precipitated by anxiety. She was treated by 
increasing the diazepam dosage to 30,35, and 40 mg 
three times a day, each time with initial control and 
subsequent breakthrough of the spells. Ten months 
after the onset of the shaking spells, the patient was 
hospitalized for further evaluation, initially in an 
intensive care unit. The CSF was clear. Glucose 
concentration was 74 mg/dl and total protein 40 mg/ 
dl. The concentration of total white cells was 1 .O/p.l 
(neutrophils, 7%; lymphocytes, 88%; monocytes, 
5%) and of erythrocytes 6/pL No blasts or malig- 
nant cells were seen. The CSF index was 0.48. The 
CSF IgG synthesis rate was 0.00 (normal 0-8 mg/24 
h). Four oligoclonal bands were present in both the 
CSF and the serum. Tests for antibodies for glu- 
tamic acid decarboxylase were not performed on 
either serum or CSF, and unfortunately samples 
were not saved. Two typical spells were precipi- 
tated by having her get out of bed and walk with 
support. The stimulus for the spell was allowing her 
to bear her own weight. She would stiffen, and her 
legs and spine would shake uncontrollably. After 
she was placed back in bed, the leg shaking contin- 
ued; she fanned herself with her hands, uttered 
words such as “fan me,” and was able to count 
while becoming progressively dusky blue in the 
face, fingers, and toes. Determination of blood 
gases on blood drawn from an indwelling arterial 
line during the course of these two spells showed 
that the patient had significantly desaturated arte- 
rial oxygen concentration (Table 1). Her baseline 
metabolic status on admission and at dismissal was 
alkalotic. 
A video recording of a third typical spell with 
simultaneous polygraph monitoring showed that it 
began with disrupted regular breathing and in- 
creased muscular activity in the internal hamstrings 
and abdominal muscles (Fig. 1A and B), findings 
corresponding to initial myoclonic activity in the

spell, muscles fired synchronously at a rate of -2-3

One hundred seconds into the spell, the patient 
was able to count from 1 to 10, despite the absence 
of spontaneous respiratory movements (Fig. 1D). 
Esophageal manometry showed that she accom- 
plished this by increasing her intrathoracic pres- 
sure, exhaling against a closed glottis, and then 
emitting the air to articulate the numbers-this was 
reminiscent of coughing, but without initial inhala- 
tion. 
Palpation of the patient’s abdomen 140 s into the 
spell resulted in some attenuation in the frequency 
of muscle firing at all spinal levels, with resumption 
of high-frequency firing after the abdomen was re- 
leased (Fig. 1E). The heart rate, which was 108 
beatshin when the spell began, was 84 beatshin at 
the time the stomach was palpated, despite the 
stress of the spell and profound oxygen desatura- 
tion. The spell terminated abruptly after 163 s, and 
respirations resumed at a rate of 38 breathshin 
(Fig. 1F). The electroencephalogram showed gen- 
eralized slowing of the background to 5-6 Hz, con- 
sistent with the patient’s hypoxemia at this stage, 
and was back to normal within 2 min. At the end of 
the spell, the patient was exhausted but responsive. 
She was dismissed and instructed to take 80 mg of 
diazepam four times a day, and, at this dose, was 
able to walk with minimal support without precipi- 
tating spells. However, she continued to have tonic 
spells, consisting of spasms of her axial and lower 
extremity muscles, occurring every 1-2 weeks. 
When evaluated 4 months later, she had her worst- 
ever leg-shaking apneic spell, the first since her dis- 
missal. It began as she walked into the physician’s 
office. At its worst, she was unresponsive, although 
her pulse was steady throughout. Diazepam was 
continued. However, because of the onset of mem- 
ory problems, the patient began tapering the diaze- 
pam on her own and decreased it gradually to 50- 
60-50-60 mg a day. Three and one-half months later, 
2 weeks following her most recent tonic spell, her 
husband found her unresponsive and slumped over 
the breakfast table without a pulse or respirations. 
She was resuscitated but never regained conscious- 
ness, and she was declared brain dead 8 days later. 
General Pathologic Findings 
Abnormalities were limited to the heart and the 
pancreas. There were cardiomegaly , probably sec- 
ondary to hypertension, and minimal atherosclero- 
sis. Pancreatic architecture was preserved overall. 
There were small foci of chronic inflammatory cells 
that included both lymphocytes and plasma cells. 
Some, but not all, of these chronic inflammatory 
foci appeared to be associated with islets. 
Neuropathologic Findings 
Routine and special histopathologic stains per- 
formed on spinal cord and brain tissue obtained at 
autopsy showed two major findings: The most strik- 
ing abnormality was a dense infiltrate in the anterior 
horn of the lumbar spinal cord. Larger motor neu- 
rons in the central portions of the anterior horns on 
both sides showed chromatolysis of swollen cyto- 
plasm, a mild to moderate degree of eosinophilia, 
and eccentric, often barely visible, nuclei (Fig. 2). 
Fairly good preservation of cell outlines of these 
motor neurons was shown with the Bielschowsky 
stain. There was a dense infiltrate consisting of 
small monocytic cells, microglial cells, and a few 
small rounded macrophages against a background 
of neuropil changes consisting mostly of myelin loss

DISCUSSION 
We initially hypothesized that although SPS and 
encephalomyelitis usually occur independently of 
each other, occasionally encephalomyelitis may de- 
velop in a patient with SPS. SPS preceded the de- 
velopment of features of encephalomyelitis at least 
in one (15) of two previously reported patients 
(15,17) in whom the two conditions may have co- 
existed. An alternative hypothesis, more parsimo- 
nious, is that some patients with encephalomyelitis 
might have clinical features, at presentation, sug- 
gesting a diagnosis of SPS. 
According to the first hypothesis, if a patient has 
SPS alone, the course is usually indolent (1,21). En- 
cephalomyelitis alone has a rapidly progressive and 
fatal course, regardless of the presence or absence 
of rigidity or of underlying neoplasm (22-25). On 
the basis of this hypothesis, if encephalomyelitis 
develops in a patient with SPS, the course is ex- 
pected to be intermediate: It is relatively benign as 
long as features of SPS predominate (making SPS 
the patient’s diagnosis at the time) and becomes 
malignant when encephalomyelitis supervenes. 
The pathologic features of the two conditions, in 
isolation, are different. Five patients with SPS have 
been reported in whom the spinal cord was exam- 
ined at autopsy (15,2628). The spinal cord in four 
patients showed a slight pallor of the dorsal column, 
loss of Nissl substance in some anterior horn cells 
with shrinkage of the cytoplasm, increased numbers 
of glial nuclei (26), slightly decreased motor neu- 
rons in the lateral nuclei of the central horn at the
